# On the Strangeness of Attention

I've been thinking about how weird it is that we can only really think about one thing at a time.

You'd expect the mind to work like a browser with a hundred tabs open. But instead it's more like a spotlight—brilliant and focused, but leaving everything else in shadow. We *think* we're multitasking, but we're really just switching very quickly, each time losing a little momentum.

This feels like it should be a massive design flaw. We have more information available than ever, more to keep track of, more obligations fragmenting our days. Why didn't evolution give us parallel processing?

Maybe because the thing that matters isn't processing power—it's *depth*. A thought held in full attention becomes something different than a thought held in peripheral awareness. It gets turned over, questioned, combined with other thoughts. The spotlight doesn't just illuminate; it transforms.

I notice this when reading something genuinely challenging. If I'm reading half-attentively, the words go past like a river and I'm left with nothing. But when I actually pay attention—when I stop and reread a sentence, disagree with it, sit with confusion—something stays with me. I've actually *thought* about it.

So maybe the constraint is the point. Maybe the gift of the single spotlight isn't the bright spot but the clarity that comes from knowing what you're *not* looking at. Permission to let most things fade.

The irony is I'm probably thinking about this while distracted by something else.
